Revamp

ree-VAMP -- from 're-' (again) plus 'vamp,' the front part of a shoe. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To revamp to give something a new and improved form.

The struggling airline hired new designers to revamp its outdated boarding process from the ground up.

Worked Example

A run-down neighborhood diner tears out its cracked booths, repaints every wall, and rewrites its entire menu, reopening a month later almost unrecognizable.

That thorough rebuilding into something better is exactly what it means to revamp something. Unlike 'repeat,' which keeps things the same, revamp changes and improves them.

How Revamp Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

overhaul

overhaul: to thoroughly repair or improve something

renovate

renovate: to restore something to a good, updated condition

modernize

modernize: to bring something up to date

Antonyms

neglect

neglect: to fail to take care of something

preserve

preserve: to keep something exactly as it was

How Strong Is It? — modernize → overhaul → revamp

modernize vs. revamp

modernize vs. revamp: Modernize is a bit narrower than revamp -- modernize specifically means updating something to match current times, while revamp can mean any kind of thorough improvement, old-fashioned or not.

overhaul vs. revamp

overhaul vs. revamp: Overhaul can feel more intense than revamp: revamp often means giving something a fresh new look or approach, while overhaul suggests taking it apart down to its core and rebuilding it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: again (Latin)

root — -vamp-

root — -vamp-: the front part of a shoe or boot (Old French (avant-pied, 'front of the foot'))

Put it together

Put it together: Vamp originally named the front part of a shoe, from Old French avant-pied, 'front of the foot.' To revamp something first meant to patch up an old shoe's worn-out front -- the same 'front, before' idea survives in vanguard, the troops placed at the very front.
